metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Trussville, AL | Jefferson County
metaDescription: Trussville, AL has grown fast over old Jefferson County mineral estates. We check Black Warrior Basin CBM history near your parcel and make a written cash offer.
heroLead: Trussville has grown into one of Jefferson County's fastest-developing suburbs, but a surprising number of new subdivisions sit over mineral estates that were reserved decades before the first house went up.
intro: Trussville's growth along the Cahaba River corridor has been mostly residential and commercial in the last two decades, but the county's coal and gas history runs deeper than the new construction suggests. When farmland or timberland around Trussville was sold to developers, it wasn't unusual for the seller's family to retain the mineral rights as a separate asset, sometimes a clause added almost as an afterthought that's now worth a real conversation.

If you're holding a mineral interest tied to land your family once owned around Trussville, we can look up the reservation, check it against current Black Warrior Basin activity, and give you a clear picture of what it's worth today.

sections.heading: New rooftops, old severed minerals
paragraphs: It's common for a Trussville-area mineral owner to have no idea a reservation exists until a title search for an unrelated transaction turns it up, or until a letter arrives referencing a decades-old deed. If that's happened to you, the interest is real even if it feels unfamiliar, and it's worth confirming exactly what you hold before deciding what to do with it.

We also see families who know they kept the minerals but assumed development on the surface made the interest irrelevant. It doesn't. Surface use and mineral value are separate questions, and a subdivision on top of your acreage doesn't erase what's below it.

sections.heading: Trussville's position relative to the CBM core
paragraphs: The most productive Black Warrior coalbed methane fields sit well southwest of Trussville, so direct production under the city itself is limited. What we look for instead is whether your legal description falls near any historic permits, old degasification wells tied to underground coal mining, or units that extended into northeast Jefferson County during the basin's more active years.

Most Trussville-area interests we evaluate end up priced as long-term speculative acreage rather than active royalty streams, and we'll tell you clearly which bucket yours falls into before we make an offer.

sections.heading: Getting a clear answer quickly
paragraphs: If you have a deed, a probate file, or even just the address of the land your family sold, that's usually enough for us to start the title work. We'll confirm the reservation, check current activity nearby, and come back with a specific number and the reasoning behind it, in writing, so you're not guessing at how we got there.

There's no obligation to sell once you have that information. A lot of Trussville owners just want to finally know what they're holding, and we're glad to provide that even if you decide to keep the interest.

faqs.question: I didn't know my family kept mineral rights near Trussville. How do I confirm it?
faqs.answer: Send us the address or legal description of the land your family sold, and we'll run a title check through Jefferson County records to confirm whether a reservation exists.

faqs.question: Does the new development on top of our old land affect the mineral value?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Mineral value is driven by subsurface geology and production potential, not what's built on the surface, though heavy development can occasionally affect future drilling access.

faqs.question: Is there active coalbed methane production right under Trussville?
faqs.answer: Trussville sits outside the historic core of Black Warrior Basin CBM activity, so we generally price interests here as speculative acreage unless your specific parcel shows nearby permits or unit history.
